title: EI? EI? Oh!
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: This article from the Mutually Assured Instruction newsletter examines the gap between teachers' initial reluctance to adopt explicit instruction (EI) and what happens after they give it a genuine try -- and why even enthusiastic early adopters often fail to sustain the shift into full implementation. The author catalogs the familiar straw-man arguments against explicit instruction (students need to discover, need to struggle, won't be engaged) and notes a recurring pattern: teachers who trial one element (mini whiteboards, a Do Now, checks for understanding) report dramatically positive student responses and become relatively converted. The catch is the word 'relatively.' The article distinguishes between treating explicit instruction as a 'toolbelt' (novelties to deploy occasionally) versus understanding it as a consolidating system of routines that becomes more effective through consistency. 'Consistency over novelty' is the article's spine: the phrase 'I'll use mini whiteboards every now and then' misunderstands why the technique works, which is precisely because routines build predictability into which deeper learning can happen. The article also examines the 'explicit instruction portion of the lesson' misconception -- the idea that EI occupies one segment of a lesson -- and argues this is a category error: explicit instruction is the entire architecture from Do Now through recap to new learning through checks for understanding, with scaffolding continuously fading toward independence throughout.
points: The typical adoption trajectory for explicit instruction: initial straw-man resistance --> trial of one element --> surprise at positive student response --> relatively-converted status, treating EI as a toolbelt of optional novelties rather than a coherent system.

The toolbelt mistake: phrases like 'I might use mini whiteboards every now and then' reveal a category error -- EI works because of the consolidation of routines over time, and deploying it occasionally severs the mechanism that produces its effect.

The 'explicit instruction portion of the lesson' phrase reflects a second category error -- EI is not a segment but the entire architecture from Do Now through recap to new learning through checks for understanding, with scaffolding fading toward independence throughout.

Only 1 in 100 teachers implements a strategy after in-school professional learning, making external expert-led sessions the more effective change driver -- internal PD suffers from being mandatory while external sessions are opt-in, reactivating adult resistance to being told what to do.

Consistency over novelty is the axiom that makes explicit instruction work: the reason students respond so well to Do Nows and mini whiteboards is their predictability, and predictability requires they not be occasional treats.
quotes: Time and time again I love hearing back from these teachers about how engaged students were when they used mini white boards or that a 'Do Now' activity meant that class started in a far calmer manner or that students who were often passive were suddenly actively involved in the lesson.

You'll hear statements like 'I used mini whiteboards last lesson and it went amazingly, I might have to plan to do that every now and then.' It makes the strategies feel like more of a novelty than an active tool of effective teaching.

The elements of explicit teaching aren't really a choose your own adventure to build a bespoke lesson framework of your own. One of the reasons why explicit teaching is so effective is because of the consolidation of routines over time. Consistency over novelty.

The 'explicit instruction portion of the lesson' is a puzzling statement which shows a great misconception about what explicit teaching actually is. If you were to come to the explicit part of my lesson you'd have to be there for the whole time.
The lesson travels from Do Now to recap to new learning and checks for understanding on a constant short cycle gradually fading scaffolding towards independence.

Only 1 in 100 teachers will actually implement a strategy when it is presented to them in an in school professional learning. When external experts have been in town and staff have been involved in their sessions it has been transformative.
